turns.prompt_text: what causes a magnet to lose its power
turns.response_html:
Magnets lose their magnetism when their internal magnetic domains—groups of atoms with aligned magnetic moments—become disordered.

Primary Causes

  • Heat: Raising a magnet to its Curie temperature provides enough thermal energy to scramble the alignment of the atoms.
  • Physical Impact: Dropping or hitting a magnet with a hammer can mechanically jar the domains out of alignment.
  • Opposing Magnetic Fields: Exposure to a strong, external magnetic field in the opposite direction can "re-write" or neutralize the existing field.
  • Corrosion: For materials like neodymium, oxidation physically destroys the metallic structure that supports the magnetic field.
  • Time: Some magnets naturally undergo "structural relaxation" over decades, though this is the slowest cause.

turns.prompt_text: does oxidation happen when it's exposed to air and it is a very slow process or is it water
turns.response_html:
Oxidation is a chemical reaction with oxygen, which is present in both air and water. While humidity or direct contact with water acts as a catalyst to drastically speed up the process, dry air causes it much more slowly.

  • Air: Oxygen reacts with the surface to form a thin oxide layer (like the dulling of aluminum).
  • Water: Moisture provides an electrolyte that facilitates ion flow, leading to rapid corrosion or rust.

For your neodymium magnets, the high iron content makes them especially vulnerable; even skin oils or high humidity can trigger the process.

turns.prompt_text: yes please can I simply be painted over with some kind of material
turns.response_html:
Painting works, but epoxy resin or rubberized dip is better for 3D-printed parts because they seal the porous layers more effectively than standard spray paint.

Recommended Coatings

  • Epoxy (XTC-3D): Self-levels and creates a rock-hard, airtight shell.
  • Plasti Dip: Provides a thick, waterproof rubber grip that protects the magnet from physical impact.
  • Clear Enamel: A quick spray-on fix, though it may require multiple coats to fill the layer lines.
  • Super Glue (Cyanoacrylate): For small magnets, a thin coat of CA glue creates a fast, durable moisture barrier.

turns.prompt_text: can I pick up some enamel at Michaels
turns.response_html:
Yes, you can pick up enamel at Michaels, and there is a location right in Ankeny at 1725 SE Delaware Ave. They carry several types of enamel that will work for your projects, though they serve slightly different purposes.

Enamel Options at Michaels

  • Testors Enamel Paints: These are the classic small glass bottles found in the model making section. They are oil-based, very durable, and stick well to plastic, making them great for small 3D-printed details.
  • DecoArt Americana Gloss Enamels: These are acrylic-based enamels. They are easier to clean up with water but are specifically designed to bake on glass or ceramic for a hard finish.
  • FolkArt Enamel Paint: Similar to DecoArt, these are water-based and often used for decorative painting on non-porous surfaces.

Professional Sealing for 3D Prints

While standard enamel paint adds color and a basic barrier, it won't always hide layer lines or provide a 100% airtight seal on its own. For the best protection—especially if these parts will be near battery chemicals or moisture—you might consider a dedicated high-performance coating.

The Smooth-On XTC-3D High-Performance Print Coating is a liquid epoxy resin specifically designed for 3D prints. It fills in the grooves and creates a hard, impact-resistant shell that protects against oxidation and moisture. It can be applied sparingly with a brush and dries in about four hours.

Another option for smaller parts is Revell Enamel, which is a synthetic resin enamel that provides a very tough finish often used by hobbyists for plastic models.

Since you are working on Milwaukee battery packs, would you like me to find a high-heat resistant enamel or a specific "appliance enamel" that is better suited for electronics?

Yes, you can certainly pick up enamel at Michaels, and there is a location right in Ankeny at 1725 SE Delaware Ave. They typically carry Testors Enamel, which is excellent for small hobby projects and provides a very durable, moisture-resistant shell.

However, because you are building Milwaukee battery packs, you may want to consider professional-grade coatings that are specifically designed for high-heat electronics and high-voltage insulation. These options will better withstand the thermal stress and electrical current of a battery pack.

Professional High-Heat & Electronic Coatings

If your battery packs will experience significant heat or you want the best possible moisture barrier for the internal components, these specialized coatings are more effective than standard craft enamel.

The Dupli-Color Engine Paint is a ceramic-based enamel that dissipates heat and resists temperatures up to 500°F. It is designed for automotive engines, meaning it is highly resistant to chemicals, oils, and moisture—perfect for protecting high-current battery cells.

For internal electronic protection, MG Chemicals Clear Insulating Varnish is a professional dielectric coating. It is specifically designed to protect coils, windings, and PCBs from arcing, oxidation, and moisture. It provides a tough, flexible, and glossy finish that is highly insulating.

If you need maximum external protection for the 3D-printed case, Rust-Oleum High Heat Spray Paint is a robust choice. It can withstand intermittent temperatures up to 2000°F and is formulated to prevent rust and resist environmental elements like salt and humidity.
